moments.title: Three forms of a straight line
moments.text: The presenter introduces gradient-intercept, point-gradient and general form, and explains that the requested form determines how to present the answer.

moments.title: Gradient-intercept form
moments.text: In $y=mx+c$, $m$ is the gradient and $c$ is the y-intercept.

moments.title: Read the intercept and gradient
moments.text: The example line has y-intercept 2 and rises 2 units for a run of 3, so its gradient is $2/3$.

moments.title: Write the equation
moments.text: Substitution gives $y=\frac23x+2$.

moments.title: When the intercept is not given
moments.text: Point-gradient form is useful when a point and the gradient are known but the intercept is not immediately available.

moments.title: Use the point and gradient
moments.text: The example line passes through $(3,4)$ with gradient $2/3$, giving $y-4=\frac23(x-3)$.

moments.title: Rearrange to general form
moments.text: Expand the brackets and collect terms on one side to obtain $-\frac23x+y-2=0$.

moments.title: Remove the fraction
moments.text: Multiplying every term by 3 gives $-2x+3y-6=0$.

moments.title: Equivalent equations
moments.text: The gradient-intercept and general-form equations describe the same line; give the form the question requests.

moments.title: Intercepts
moments.text: An x-intercept lies on the horizontal axis; a y-intercept lies on the vertical axis.

moments.title: Gradient as steepness
moments.text: The presenter introduces gradient as rise divided by run.

moments.title: Read two intercepts
moments.text: The first example passes through $(0,2)$ and $(4,0)$.

moments.title: Calculate the gradient
moments.text: Using the two points gives $(0-2)/(4-0)=-1/2$. The gradient is negative because the line falls from left to right.

moments.title: Find another gradient
moments.text: For points $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$, the gradient is 2 and the y-intercept is 1.

moments.title: Find an unknown x-intercept
moments.text: Write $y=2x+1$, set $y=0$ and solve to obtain the x-intercept $(-1/2,0)$.

moments.title: Summarise intercepts and gradient
moments.text: The presenter recaps intercepts and the two-point gradient formula.

notes.title: Horizontal and vertical lines
notes.text: The recap says a straight line has one x-intercept and one y-intercept. Horizontal and vertical lines can be exceptions.
notes.write: For example, $y=2$ has no x-intercept; $x=3$ has no y-intercept. The coordinate axes themselves have infinitely many intercept points on the axis they coincide with.

moments.title: Parallel lines
moments.text: Distinct parallel nonvertical lines have equal gradients.

moments.title: Perpendicular lines
moments.text: Perpendicular nonvertical lines with defined gradients have gradients that are negative reciprocals.

moments.title: Identify the relationships
moments.text: Line A has gradient 2, line B is parallel to A and line C is perpendicular to A.

moments.title: Find the parallel gradient
moments.text: Line B has gradient 2, the same as line A.

moments.title: Find the perpendicular gradient
moments.text: The negative reciprocal of 2 is $-1/2$, so line C has gradient $-1/2$.

moments.title: Compare the rules
moments.text: Equal gradients indicate parallel nonvertical lines; a product of $-1$ indicates perpendicular nonvertical lines.

notes.title: Vertical and horizontal lines
notes.text: The negative-reciprocal formula assumes both gradients are defined.
notes.write: A vertical line has undefined gradient and is perpendicular to a horizontal line, whose gradient is zero.

ican.text: I can find a gradient from two points and interpret its sign and units.
I can write and convert between gradient-intercept, point-gradient and general forms of a straight line.
I can find and interpret x- and y-intercepts, including situations where an intercept does not exist.
I can determine gradients and equations of parallel and perpendicular lines.
I can handle horizontal and vertical lines without applying a formula that divides by zero.
I can interpret the gradient and intercept of a linear model in context.

ku.text: For two points with $x_1\ne x_2$, the gradient is $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$. Preserve the same order in numerator and denominator.
A nonvertical line may be written $y=mx+c$ or $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$. A general form is $ax+by+d=0$, where $a$ and $b$ are not both zero.
At an x-intercept $y=0$; at a y-intercept $x=0$. Interpret each coordinate in context rather than assuming an intercept is meaningful in the domain.
Distinct parallel nonvertical lines have equal gradients. Two nonvertical lines with nonzero gradients are perpendicular when $m_1m_2=-1$.
A horizontal line $y=k$ has gradient 0. A vertical line $x=h$ has undefined gradient; every horizontal line is perpendicular to every vertical line.
For a model $y=mx+c$, the gradient describes the change in $y$ per one-unit increase in $x$, with units. The intercept is the modelled value of $y$ at $x=0$, provided that input is meaningful.

misc.weak: A line perpendicular to gradient $3/2$ has gradient $-3/2$.
Every straight line has both an x-intercept and a y-intercept.
misc.better: A nonzero horizontal line has no x-intercept; a nonzero vertical line has no y-intercept. The axes themselves are special cases.
A vertical line has undefined gradient because its horizontal change is zero. A horizontal line has gradient 0.

misc.weak: A point-gradient equation $y-2=\frac32(x-1)$ is invalid because it is not in $y=mx+c$ form.
misc.better: It is an equation of the line. Rearrange only when the question requests another form.

misc.weak: Multiply only the fractional term when clearing denominators in an equation.
misc.better: Multiply every term on both sides by the same nonzero number.

terms.text: Use a point and gradient, or use an intercept and gradient. Give the requested form and check the original point.
Set the other coordinate equal to zero; state the coordinates or values in the form requested.
Describe the change in the dependent quantity for one unit of the independent quantity, including units.
Use the appropriate gradient relationship and then a point on the required line; treat vertical and horizontal lines separately.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find an equation of $L$ in the form $ax+by+d=0$ with integer coefficients.
parts.a: $y-2=\frac32(x-1)$, so $y=\frac32x+\frac12$. Multiplying by 2 and rearranging gives $3x-2y+1=0$. Any nonzero multiple is equivalent.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Find the coordinates of the intercepts of $L$.
parts.a: Set $x=0$ to get $(0,1/2)$. Set $y=0$ to obtain $x=-1/3$, so the x-intercept is $(-1/3,0)$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: A line perpendicular to $L$ passes through $(2,-1)$. Find its equation.

parts.label: (e)
parts.q: A separate taxi model is $C=150t+1200$, where $t$ is hours and $C$ is cost in baht. Interpret the gradient and intercept.
parts.a: The model adds 150 baht for each additional hour. At $t=0$, the model's cost is 1200 baht, the fixed starting cost in this context.

kq.q: Why does reversing both points in the gradient formula give the same result?
kq.model: Both the change in $y$ and the change in $x$ change sign, so their ratio remains unchanged.

kq.q: Why can a vertical line not be written as $y=mx+c$ with a finite gradient?
kq.model: Its horizontal change is zero, so rise divided by run is undefined. Its equation has the form $x=h$.

kq.q: Why do nonzero perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$?
kq.model: For two nonvertical perpendicular lines the gradients are negative reciprocals: $m_2=-1/m_1$, so $m_1m_2=-1$.

kq.q: Why might an intercept be mathematically correct but not meaningful in context?
kq.model: The intercept describes the model at an input or output of zero. That point may lie outside the model's realistic domain or have no practical interpretation.
